d: A subordinate deity, in some philosophies the creator of the universe
ety: From Ancient Greek δημιουργός (dēmiourgós, “one who works for the people; a skilled workman, a handicraftsman”) (whence Latin dēmiūrgus, French démiurge), from δήμιος (dḗmios, “belonging to the people, public”) (from δῆμος (dêmos, “the people”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂mos (“people”), from *deh₂- (“to divide”) + Ancient Greek -ιος (-ios), from Proto-Indo-European *-yós (suffix creating an ad
s: A demiurge or craftsman god takes pre-existing matter and fashions it in light of the eternal Forms.

d: A disreputable or clumsy man
ety: From Quranic Arabic جالُوت (jālūt, pronounced galūt in Egyptian Arabic), proper name equivalent to English Goliath, giant warrior of the ancient Philistine ethnicity; cf. connotations of derogatory uses of English Philistine. Doublet of goliath.
s: “So if someone does something I do not agree with, I could call him a galoot and it would be okay?” “Something like that, if you were friends.” “Are galoots always men?”

d: Conspicuously and offensively loud; given to vehement outcry
ety: From French strident, from Latin strīdēns, present active participle of strīdō.
s: The trumpet sounded strident against the string orchestra.

d: An agricultural laborer in Arab countries
ety: Borrowed from Arabic فَلَّاح (fallāḥ, “peasant”), from Classical Syriac ܦܠܚܐ (“worker; peasant”). Attested since 1743.
s: 1929-1930, H P Lovecraft, Fungi from Yuggoth And at the last from inner Egypt came // The strange dark One to whom the fellahs bowed

d: Grant in a condescending manner
ety: From vouch + safe, written as two words in Middle English and early Modern English.
s: She vouchsafed to me that she regretted ever marrying him.

d: An important or influential (and often overbearing) person
ety: Coined as a nonce word in the 18th century by British dramatist Samuel Foote.
s: Silicon Valley panjandrums spent the 2010s lecturing American workers in dying industries that they needed to “learn to code.”

d: A slight convexity (as of the surface of a road)
ety: From Old French cambre (“bent”), from Latin camurum, from camur (“arched”).
s: The track was stony with a grassy camber up the middle.

d: Of noxious stench from atmospheric pollution
ety: From Latin mephīticus, from mephītis; compare French méphitique.
s: "I could have borne the sight of his crutch," said she, "but the crutch and the nephew together really oppress me like a mephitic vapour."

d: Capable of reflecting light like a mirror
ety: From Latin speculāris, from speculum; and in some senses from speculārī (“to watch, observe”). Some later senses via French spéculaire.
s: Thy specular orb / Apply to well-dissected kernels; lo! / In each observe the slender threads / Of first-beginning trees.

d: Smiling with happiness or optimism
ety: From beam + -ish.
s: But oh, beamish nephew, beware of the day, If your Snark be a Boojum!

d: An incorrect or unsuitable name
ety: The noun is derived from Late Middle English misnoumer (“(law) mistaken identification of a person; plea based on such misidentification”), from Anglo-Norman mesnomer, a noun use of Anglo-Norman mesnomer, mesnommer, and Old French mesnomer, mesnommer (“to name incorrectly”), from mes- (prefix meaning ‘badly, wrongly’) + nomer, nommer (“to name”) (from Latin nōmināre, the present active infinitive
s: It’s a misnomer that all doctors have bad handwriting.

d: Model of excellence or perfection of a kind; one having no equal
ety: From Late Middle English non-parail (“unparalleled, nonpareil”) [and other forms], from Middle French nonpareille, nonpareil (“unparalleled”) (obsolete), from non- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + pareil (“alike, like, same”). Pareil is derived from Old French pareil, from Late Latin pāriculus (“equal; like; of a number: even”), from Latin pār (“equal; like; of a number: even; suitable”) + -culus (a varia
s: My lord and master loves you. O, such love / Could be but recompens'd though you were crown'd / The nonpareil of beauty!

d: A conceited dandy who is overly impressed by his own accomplishments
ety: From Middle English cokke’s comb.
s: And she nearly started a fight between two young fops in plumed hats and flouncy collars: "Clay-brained coxcomb!" "Mewling milk-livered maggot!"

d: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility; not easily aroused or excited
ety: From Middle French stolide, from Latin stolidus (“foolish, obtuse, slow”).
s: “A tinge of Jewish blood is not a bad thing. It leavens the”—she looked at him—“stolid stupidity of the ordinary Englishman.”

d: An architectural support or base (as for a column or statue)
ety: From French plinthe, from Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).
s: The queen placed the vase on the plinth so the cupbearer could fill it with flowers.

d: A person who has taught himself
ety: From Ancient Greek αὐτοδίδακτος (autodídaktos), from αὐτός (autós, “self”) + διδάσκω (didáskō, “I teach”). By surface analysis, auto- + didact.
s: Leonardo Da Vinci is one of the greatest autodidacts.

d: Having or showing arrogant superiority to and disdain of those one views as unworthy
ety: From Latin imperiōsus (“mighty, powerful”), from imperium (“command, authority, power”).
s: She was quick, beautiful, imperious, while he was quiet, slow, and misty.

d: A comic incident or series of incidents
ety: From French drôlerie, from drôle + -erie; equivalent to droll + -ery.
s: "I'm pregnant." "No drolleries this morning please." "Three months."

d: The first name of a citizen of ancient Rome
ety: From Latin praenōmen, from prae- (“pre-: before”) + nōmen (“name, family name”).
s: Julius Caesar's praenomen was Gaius.

d: An illusory feat; considered magical by naive observers
ety: From Middle English legerdemeyn, lechardemane, from Old French léger de main (literally “light of hand”), a phrase that meant “dexterous, skillful at fooling others (especially through sleights of hand)”, which was however treated as a noun when it was borrowed by late Middle English. The Modern French descendant léger de main of the Old French phrase is archaic but still sometimes found in older
s: Just for a moment, absurdly over-estimating poor Zuleika’s skill, he supposed himself a victim of legerdemain.

d: Panel forming the lower part of an interior wall when it is finished differently from the rest of the wall
ety: From Middle English waynscot, from Middle Low German wagenschot or Middle Dutch waghenscote, assumed to be from wagen (“wagon”) (from Old Saxon wagan) + schot, meaning “partition, crossbar," which is from or related to skiotan (“to shoot”).
s: Entering that gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wainscots, reminding one of the bulwarks of some condemned old craft.

d: A justly deserved penalty
ety: From requite + -al. First attested in 1545.
s: O, take his mother's thanks, a widow's thanks, / Till your strong hand shall help to give him strength / To make a more requital to your love.

d: Liberality in bestowing gifts; extremely liberal and generous of spirit
ety: From Middle French munificence, from Latin munificentia, from munus (“gift”) + facio (“to make”).
s: Untill that Locrine for his Realmes defence, Did head against them make and strong munificence

d: Not produced by natural forces
ety: Borrowed from Latin factītius (“artificial”), alternative form of factīcius, from faciō (“to make, do”). Doublet of fetish.
s: Manners are partly factitious, but, mainly, there must be capacity for culture in the blood. Else all culture is vain.

d: Work of little or no value done merely to look busy
ety: Coined by American scout leader Robert H. Link in 1929; alternatively “boon doggle”. Compare woggle of similar sense, which is attested in the same period. In the sense of a “wasteful government program”, popularized in 1935 by The New York Times, in reference to New Deal programs which were claimed to feature people making such braids.
s: Opponents consider this another billion-dollar government boondoggle.

d: A behavioral attribute that is distinctive and peculiar to an individual
ety: 1640–50, from Early Modern French foible (“feeble”) (contemporary French faible). Doublet of feeble.
s: Try to look past his foibles and see the friendly fellow underneath.

d: Marked by quiet and caution and secrecy; taking pains to avoid being observed
ety: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft; robbery”) (from fūr (“thief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives).
s: The proprietor of the house cowered over a bed-candle and a furtive tea-pot in the back drawing-room.

d: Purchased; not homemade
ety: From bought + -en (past participle ending of some verbs).
s: “Well, it’s nothin’ at all in the world,” said she, “only I strongly expect Miss Niles drinks boughten tea, and if I knew she did, I’d never set my foot in her house again.”

d: At right angles to the center line of a ship
ety: From Late Middle English athwert, athirt, from a- (prefix meaning ‘in the direction of, toward’) + thwert (“crosswise; (cooking) across the grain”, adverb). Thwert is derived from thwert (“crosswise, transverse; counter, opposing; contrary, obstinate, stubborn”, adjective), borrowed from Old Norse þvert (“across, athwart”), originally the neuter form of þverr (“across, transverse”), from Proto-Ger
s: Above, the stars appeared to move slowly athwart.

d: Verbal misrepresentation intended to take advantage of you in some way
ety: An alteration of Scots sculduddery, sculdudrie (“adultery, unchaste behaviour; obscenity, lewdness”), of long-uncertain origin (probably a euphemism). Relation to skull is speculative at best and likely folk etymology. The American spelling skullduggery is in keeping with terms such as skillful and willful.
s: How did Hercules (Herc. of antiquity) slay the Hydrant and cleanse the stables of Oregon? Did it all by main force, didn't he? Power? Shenanigan? Skulduggery? Of course he did.

d: A song in which a line or phrase is repeated as the refrain
ety: From Middle French rondelet, diminutive of Old French rondel (French: rondeau). Ending -lay either from lay (“ballad or sung poem”), or from virelay.
s: It fell upon a holly eve, Hey ho, hollidaye! When holly fathers wont to shrieve, Now gynneth this roundelay.

d: A pomade to make the hair manageable and lustrous
ety: Borrowed from French brillantine.
s: The hairdresser's shop was warm and glittering. It smelled of soap and burnt paper and wallflower brilliantine.

d: A shackle for the ankles or feet
ety: From Middle English feter, from Old English feter, Proto-West Germanic *fetur, from Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”). Related to foot. Cognates Cognate with Dutch veter (“cable, chain, hawser; bond, fetter”), Faroese fjøtur (“fetter”), Icelandic fjötur (“fetter”), Swedish fjätter (“fetter, shackle”); also Irish feadh (“extent, l
s: Passion's too fierce to be in fetters bound.

d: Full of or showing high-spirited merriment
ety: From Old French jocond, from Latin iūcundus (“pleasant, agreeable”). Doublet of jucund.
s: I was feeling blithe, almost jocund.

d: The exclusive right of a country to control the air traffic within its borders
ety: Borrowed from French cabotage (“coasting trade”), from caboter (“to travel by the coast”). It originally (16th c.) referred to restrictions allowing only French ships to trade or transport between French ports. Other countries adopted this concept and extended it to land and air travel.
s: Cabotage, used as a legal term, here refers to the right to transport goods or passengers between ports of a country.

d: A comic verse of irregular measure
ety: Probably from dog + -rel (“pejorative suffix”), akin to Dog Latin, late 14th c.
s: As he marched he sang a bit of doggerel in a high and quavering voice: / "Sing a song 'a vic'try, / A pocketful 'a bullets, / Five an' twenty dead men / Baked in a—pie."

d: A long boring tediously detailed account
ety: From Hebrew מגילה / מְגִלָּה (m'gilá, “scroll”). Doublet of magilla.
s: Actually, a monetary policy maker would probably be okay with the whole “improved credibility” megillah, since it flatters their self-image.

d: Rapid simultaneous discharge of firearms
ety: From French fusillade, from fusiller (“shoot with a firearm”), from fusil (“rifle, gun”).
s: Our fusillade from the left flank caught them by surprise.

d: An almost pleasurable sensation of fright
ety: Borrowed from French frisson.
s: I felt a frisson just as they were about to announce the winner in my category.

d: Not appropriate in application; defective
ety: From in- + felicitous.
s: "Now, you've got just grounds for shooting me," he said gaily, and instantly regretted his infelicitous remark.
